messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The accident happened twelve months ago, on a cold November night. David, a 52-year-old film director, was driving home from a late location scout through a winding mountain pass when a deer bounded into his headlights. He swerved, the car left the road, and for what he later estimated as three or four seconds, he was certain he was going to die as the vehicle tumbled down an embankment, finally landing upside down against a cluster of pines. He hung suspended by his seatbelt in the dark, the smell of gasoline thick in the air, unable to move for what felt like an eternity until a passing motorist spotted the wreckage. What stayed with him most vividly were not the events in any logical sequence, but isolated images—the deer's eyes in the headlights, the dashboard crumpling toward his chest, the absolute silence after the car stopped moving. These memories were so clear and detailed that they felt more real than the present moment, and yet he found himself unable to put any of it into words when his partner asked what had happened; the pictures in his mind had no language attached to them.

In the months that followed, David began to notice that these intrusive images were triggered most powerfully by unexpected or loud sounds—a car backfiring on set, a door slamming in the editing suite, even the sharp crack of a slate at the beginning of a take. Each time, his body would react before his mind could catch up: his heart would pound, he would jump or startle in a way that embarrassed him, and he would find himself scanning the room, watching for threats that were not there. He came to believe that his reactions since the event proved he was a lousy coper, that his inability to shake the fear meant he was fundamentally inadequate. The person he had become—jumpy, withdrawn, unable to concentrate—was unrecognizable to him. These appraisals deepened every time a memory surfaced, because the very fact that the images kept coming felt like evidence of his failure to move on. He began to think constantly about why the event had happened to him, as if finding a reason might restore the version of himself he had lost.

David's work as a film director became a minefield. He started avoiding circumstances that reminded him of the accident, which meant refusing to shoot night scenes or any sequence involving driving or darkness. He told his producers it was a creative choice, but the truth was that the thought of being in the dark, even on a well-lit soundstage, made his chest tighten. When he could not avoid a triggering situation, he distracted himself—checking his phone, reviewing call sheets, focusing on technical details—anything to keep his mind occupied and the images at bay. But the distraction only worked for moments, and afterward the memories would return with renewed force, as if his efforts to push them away had only made them hungrier. And each time he relied on these strategies, he felt more convinced of his inadequacy: a real director, a strong person, would not need to hide from his own job.

The cycle tightened over weeks. His hypervigilance on set made him irritable with crew members, and he began delegating more and more of his hands-on work to his assistant director, staying in the editing bay where it was quiet and controlled. At home, his partner noticed he no longer wanted to watch films in the dark living room, preferring to sit in the kitchen with all the lights on. The startle responses to ordinary sounds—the microwave beeping, a car horn outside—became so frequent that David started wearing noise-canceling headphones even when he was not working, a small concession that made him feel pathetic but also necessary. His constant alertness, in turn, drove him deeper into avoidance: if being in certain places or hearing certain sounds could set off the fear, the only logical response was to narrow his world until nothing could surprise him. He began to think about why the event had happened, turning it over in his mind like a stone, searching for a meaning that would make the fear stop. What frightened him most was not the accident itself anymore, but the sense that he was dissolving into someone he did not recognize, someone who jumped at shadows and could no longer do the work he loved.

What finally brought David to seek help was a single moment on set two weeks ago. A grip dropped a C-stand, and the clatter sent David diving behind a monitor, his hands over his head, in full view of twenty crew members. The silence that followed was worse than the sound. He walked off set and did not return. That night, sitting in his kitchen with his partner's hand on his arm, he admitted he could not keep living this way—jumping at sounds, hiding from the dark, feeling like a stranger in his own life. He was terrified that therapy would confirm what he already suspected: that he was too broken to fix. But he was more terrified of what would happen if he did not try.
